en: The Sūtra on the Rebirths in the Five Realms and the Retribution of Sin and Merit, spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Liu Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
when the nine-month summer retreat had concluded, the Buddha emerged from his meditation chamber and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

Between the two countries there was a great tree called the Nyagrodha; it was one hundred and twenty li in height, and its branches and leaves covered an area sixty li in circumference. Upon that tree were tens of millions of bushels of fruit; when eaten, they were fragrant and sweet, their flavor like honey.
The sweet fruits ripened and fell, and when the people ate them, their various ailments were cured and their vision became clear and sharp.
As the Buddha sat beneath the tree, the bhikṣus at that time gathered the fruits and ate them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I observe that among the heavens, the earth, and all things, each has its own past affinity.
Ānanda immediately stepped forward, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What was their past affinity?
These disciples wish to hear it; please explain it fully so as to enlighten those who have not yet heard it!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If you wish to hear it, listen well with a focused mind.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When a person performs meritorious deeds, it is like this tree: originally planted from a single seed, it gradually grows large until it yields limitless fruit.”
If one is noble and wealthy as a king or an elder, it comes from having paid homage to the Buddha and served the Triple Gem;
if one is a person of great wealth with limitless possessions, it comes from practicing generosity;
if one is long-lived, free from illness, and possesses a robust physique, it comes from maintaining the precepts.

He is upright in person, with a wondrously beautiful complexion and a radiance unsurpassed; his body is supple and his breath is fragrant and pure. When people behold his countenance, there are none who do not rejoice, gazing upon him without weariness;
this comes from the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). He is cultivated in conduct, free from indolence, and delights in performing meritorious deeds;

this comes from the practice of diligence (*vīrya*). He is composed and serene, and his speech and actions are deliberate and precise; this comes from the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

He is a person of brilliant talent, who understands and penetrates the profound Dharma, praises the wondrous meaning, and awakens the ignorant; when people hear his words, there are none who do not consult him and receive his teachings, regarding them as precious jewels that have emerged from wisdom.
His voice is clear and penetrating, having emerged from the chanting of the Three Jewels.
He is pure and free from all illness, having emerged from a heart of loving-kindness.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
“What is loving-kindness?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"First, to love all sentient beings as a mother loves her child;
second, to feel compassion for the world, desiring to lead them toward the resolve for the path of liberation;
third, to have a mind that is always joyful."
"Fourth, by being able to protect and mindfully guard them, they do not transgress anything.
This is what it means to possess a mind of loving-kindness.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"One becomes tall and large because one was respectful toward others;
one becomes short and small because one was contemptuous toward others;
one becomes ugly and deformed because one delighted in anger."
One will be born ignorant because one did not pursue learning;
one will be exclusively foolish because one did not teach others;
and one will be mute because one slandered and defamed others.
One becomes deaf and blind because one did not delight in hearing and receiving the sutras and the Dharma;
one becomes a slave because one failed to repay debts;
one becomes lowly and base because one did not pay reverence to the Triple Gem.
One is born ugly and black because one obstructed the Buddha’s radiance;
one is born in a land of naked people because one delighted in lightly tossing garments over stupas, temples, and monasteries;
one is born in a land of horse-hoofed people because one delighted in wearing wooden clogs while walking before the Buddha.
Those born among the people of the Chest-Piercing Kingdom do so because they gave alms and performed meritorious deeds with a mind of regret and stinginess;
those born among deer, fawns, and muntjacs do so because they delighted in startling and frightening people;
and those born fallen among dragons do so because they delighted in mocking and playing with people.
If one develops malignant sores on the body that are difficult to cure, it is because in previous lives they delighted in whipping sentient beings without justification;
if people see them with joy, it is because in previous lives they saw others with joy;
if people see them without joy, it is because in previous lives they saw others without pleasure.

Those who encounter government officials and are imprisoned in gaols, their bodies bound with shackles and fetters, did so because in previous lives they confined sentient beings in cages against their will.
Those born with cleft lips did so because in previous lives they were fishermen and caused the mouths of fish to gape open.

Those who hear pleasant words and virtuous speech yet find no joy in hearing them, and who in the midst of such things engage in double-tongued speech to disrupt others from receiving and hearing the sutras and the Dharma, will later fall among the dogs known as "Dān-er" (the drooling-eared).
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There are foolish people in the world who, upon hearing the Dharma being preached, do not take it to heart or practice it; they later fall among the long-eared donkeys and horses.
Those who are stingy and greedy, eating alone and not sharing with the hungry, after death fall among the hungry ghosts."

Born as a human being, one is impoverished and hungry; clothing does not cover the body and food does not suffice for the mouth. One eats fine food oneself while giving coarse food to others, and subsequently is reborn among pigs, hogs, and dung beetles.
Those who take pleasure in plundering the property of others will later fall among sheep, being skinned alive as they are born to repay their past offenses;
those who delight in killing living beings will later become ephemeral insects on the water, born in the morning and dying by evening;
those who delight in stealing the wealth and goods of others will later fall among slaves, oxen, or horses, repaying their past debts.

Those who take pleasure in violating the wives and daughters of others will, upon death, enter hell; men shall embrace copper pillars and women shall lie upon iron beds. Emerging from hell, they will always be reborn in lowly places, destined to fall among chickens and ducks.

Those who take pleasure in lying and spreading evil reports about others will, upon death, enter hell; molten copper shall be poured into their mouths, their tongues shall be pulled out and plowed with oxen. Upon emerging, they fall among owls, hawks, and nightjars; when people hear their cries, none fail to be struck with terror, all exclaiming them to be portents of calamity and casting spells to bring about their death.

Those who take pleasure in drinking alcohol and commit the thirty-six transgressions will, upon death, fall into the *naraka* hell of boiling excrement; when reborn, they will fall among the *śiṃśumāra* (crocodiles), and later, returning to human form, they will be born foolish and ignorant, with husbands and wives living in discord, frequently quarreling and driving each other away, before finally falling among pigeons;
those who covet the labor of others will later fall among elephants.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"The magistrates and officials of the provinces and commanderies consume official ranks and emoluments; yet they may punish those who are innocent, or they may privately encroach upon the people by recording their names and binding them, flogging and beating them with whips and staves, and forcibly compelling them to transport goods. Having no place to appeal for redress, these people are placed in shackles and fetters and imprisoned, not being allowed any leniency. Later, they fall into hell where they undergo physical suffering;

only after thousands of billions of years, when their retribution is exhausted, do they emerge, only to fall among water buffaloes, having their noses pierced to be led in boats or pulled in carts, struck and beaten with heavy clubs as they repay their past offenses."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Those who are impure in their conduct come from among pigs;
those who are stingy and greedy, unable to be upright and pure, come from among dogs."
Those who are stubborn and headstrong, perverse and self-opinionated, come from among sheep;
those who are foul-smelling and rank, come from among fish and turtles;
those who are fierce and cruel, harboring poisonous hearts that are difficult to resolve, come from among vipers.

Those who delight in fine foods and take pleasure in killing sentient beings without a heart of compassion come from among jackals, wolves, foxes, and hawks. As humans, they are short-lived; their fetuses are injured or miscarried, and having been born for only a brief time, they meet an early end, falling into the three miserable realms for many tens of millions of kalpas.
The Buddha said:

"These people were, in their previous lives, human beings who delighted in hunting; they set fires to the mountains and marshes, probed nests and broke eggs, and laid out fishing nets to kill all living beings. Greedily consuming their skins and flesh for their own sustenance, they receive the retribution of short lifespans, with no prospect of escape for many successive kalpas."
Be cautious! Be cautious!
The pain is beyond words.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In performing meritorious deeds, one must always act with one's own body—burning incense, holding assemblies for blessings, reciting scriptures, and practicing the Way. One must not employ others; if the prayers of benediction are empty, it is like eating food on behalf of another: how could one satisfy oneself, and would one not remain hungry?"
If one offers pure and fresh incense, one will attain *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), for the fragrance encompasses all marks;
by lighting lamps to maintain the light, one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), free from all hindrances.
They made it their constant practice to burn incense, partake of vegetarian meals, recite the sutras, and offer alms;
through such giving they obtained blessings, were welcomed by the various devas, all manner of evils were repelled, and all demons were utterly eliminated, with none daring to oppose them.

A person who is indolent may enjoy peace and prosperity while lacking a mind for diligence; yet when suddenly stricken by illness or encountering some inauspicious event, they immediately wish to burn incense, only then claiming to be performing meritorious deeds.

Before the various devas have descended and while the hosts of Māras still stand before you, they will vie with one another to harass and provoke you, manifesting all manner of strange transformations.

For this reason, you must always be diligent; for sin and merit follow the person like a shadow follows a form. One who plants the seeds of merit is like the nyagrodha tree: from the planting of a single seed, the harvest of fruit is limitless. To give once and receive ten thousandfold in return—this saying is not false!
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The wise person delights in giving; The devas themselves support and guide them.
By giving one thing, one gains ten thousandfold; Peace, happiness, and a long life are attained."
Today’s great act of giving brings forth merit beyond measure;
all shall attain the Way of the Buddha and deliver beings throughout the ten directions.
When causes and conditions converge, who is truly one's kin?
Observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds, eliminating anger; do not seek others' approval, but act as your own kin. Worldly glory and pleasure are like floating clouds.
Wandering through the five realms of existence like a turning wheel, do not calculate the length of your life or begrudge gold and silver;
for even heaven and earth will perish, how much more so this body?
To uphold the sutras and precepts is a great treasure.
Do not covet wealth or beauty, which bring disgrace and delude men;

sentient beings in the three realms are like a flock of sheep, coming and going through the five paths with their bodies broken and wounded. Life is as swift as flowing water—how can it have permanence?
Committing evil brings swift retribution, for the punishment lasts long;
in the hells of the boiling cauldron, one must restrain the mind and fortify the will to escape calamity, for once a crime is committed and one enters therein, the pain is unbearable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The people of the world lack wisdom; with their physical eyes of birth and death, they do not know the retribution of sin and merit.

With my eye of the Way, I behold the retribution for sins and merits from incalculable kalpas until this present life, as clearly as observing a lapis lazuli bead in the palm of one's hand, transparent inside and out, free from any thought of doubt."
Ānanda stepped forward, adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying,
"What should this sutra be called when it is expounded?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Cycle of the Five Destinies' and is also titled 'The Retribution of Sin and Merit.

If there are good men or good women who recite and propagate it, their merit shall be immeasurable; they shall behold and serve the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, attending upon and making offerings to them, never falling into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions, and attaining morality, concentration, and wisdom."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind;
seven hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the stage of srotāpanna;
and eight hundred arhats attained the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as twelve thousand laymen and six thousand laywomen who had pure faith beneath the tree, all attained the fruits of the Path;
and all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world, having heard the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma,
all exclaimed, “Excellent!
They immediately rose and paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed with joy.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Rebirths in the Five Realms and the Retribution of Sin and Merit.
